title: The Locker of Maple Street
premise: Oscar Fairweather, the only out teenager in the fading town of Halloway, has spent senior year keeping their head down until a college essay prompt—'What truth have you been asked to carry?'—cracks something open. Digging for material, Oscar finds a locker on Maple Street stuffed with decades of school board records: hushed-up bullying deaths, vanished students, and payoffs that built the town's beloved football dynasty. As Oscar publishes what they find under a pseudonym, friendships fracture, their best friend's father turns out to be complicit, and the board moves to destroy the evidence—and Oscar's future. In the end, Oscar must choose between an anonymous escape to college and standing publicly in the gymnasium where it all began; they choose to sign their name, and the town, reluctantly and imperfectly, begins to listen.
about_author: Dominic Iversen is a former small-town newspaper reporter who spent three years covering school boards across rural Minnesota before turning to fiction. They write young adult stories about kids who refuse to wait politely for permission.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Ways to Disappear
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Establishes Halloway: the diner, the water tower, the way conversations stop when Oscar enters. Oscar counts days to graduation and rehearses invisibility. Emotional beat: weary self-containment with a hairline fracture of longing.

chapters.title: The Prompt
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. English teacher Ms. Okafor assigns a college essay: 'What truth have you been asked to carry?' Oscar freezes at the blank page, then writes one honest sentence and hates how good it feels. Beat: fear meeting appetite.

chapters.title: Denny
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Best friend Denny Kowalczyk drags Oscar to the abandoned Fairweather family property on Maple Street—Oscar's late grandmother's house, slated for demolition. Banter masks Denny's own tension about his father, a school board member. Beat: loyalty as refuge.

chapters.title: Locker 114
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the house's mudroom stands an old student locker Grandma Fairweather salvaged when the school renovated in 1987. It's locked. Oscar pries it open and finds folders, cassette tapes, and a ledger. Beat: vertigo—the past reaching up.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, intercut with 1980s letters. The documents show the board paid settlements over injuries hidden from families, all tied to Coach Brandt's football program. Oscar recognizes a name: a boy who 'moved away' in 1991. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Essay That Isn't
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar tries to write the college essay about the locker but can't without exposing everything. Ms. Okafor reads the draft and says, 'This is bigger than an essay.' Beat: the personal becoming public.

chapters.title: Denny's House
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Dinner with his father, Board Member Ray Kowalczyk, who praises Coach Brandt and dismisses 'troublemakers' digging up old grievances. Denny realizes his dad's name is in the ledger he hasn't seen yet. Beat: love and suspicion sharing a table.

chapters.title: The Pseudonym
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar starts an anonymous blog, 'The Locker,' posting scanned documents piece by piece. First post goes unnoticed; second gets forty comments overnight. Beat: intoxicating power, first taste.

chapters.title: Rosa Remembers
chapters.summary: Rosa Delgado's POV, class of 1992. A diner waitress reads the blog and recognizes her brother Mateo—the boy who 'moved away.' She calls the number Oscar left. Beat: grief finding a door.

chapters.title: Two Truths
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Rosa gives Oscar Mateo's letters describing a hazing injury the coach called 'a fall.' Oscar hides the interview from Denny, telling himself it's protection. Beat: the first deliberate lie.

chapters.title: Board Meeting, Public Comment
chapters.summary: Alternating Oscar and Denny POV. Oscar attends the board meeting posing as a journalism student; Ray Kowalczyk deflects questions with practiced warmth. Denny watches Oscar ask them and feels the floor tilt. Beat: masks slipping in fluorescent light.

chapters.title: The Essay Prompt Again
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Ms. Okafor returns essays; she's figured out who runs the blog and warns Oscar: 'Anonymity protects you until it isolates you.' Oscar bristles. Beat: mentor friction, pride inflamed.

chapters.title: Homecoming
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The whole town celebrates the football dynasty while Oscar holds the ledger in a backpack under the bleachers. A near-miss with Coach Brandt himself—charming, watchful. Beat: two towns occupying one night.

chapters.title: Denny Finds Out
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Denny matches handwriting on the blog to Oscar's notebook and confronts him in the locker room. Oscar admits everything except the part about Ray. Beat: betrayal's first cut, self-inflicted.

chapters.title: The Deal Offered
chapters.summary: Ray Kowalczyk's POV. Ray quietly offers Oscar's family money for the Maple Street property—generous, urgent. He never mentions the blog. Both understand. Beat: corruption as politeness.

chapters.title: Mateo's Tape
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar plays a 1991 cassette: Mateo's voice, sixteen years old, describing the hazing and begging someone to believe him. Oscar cries alone in the car. Beat: the dead boy becomes real.

chapters.title: Going Steady
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The blog hits the regional paper; a reporter calls. Oscar juggles interviews as 'The Locker' while classmates speculate wildly. Popularity arrives sideways—people are nice to Oscar for the first time. Beat: belonging bought with a mask.

chapters.title: Priya
chapters.summary: Priya Chandrasekaran's POV. Editor of the school paper, Priya deduces Oscar's identity and doesn't expose it—she asks to help. She's hungry for a real story and tired of fluff. Beat: alliance, transactional at first.

chapters.title: The Records Room
chapters.summary: Priya and Oscar's POV alternating. They break into the school annex after hours and photograph minutes from 1988–1994. An alarm trips; they flee through the woods, laughing and terrified. Beat: complicity as intimacy.

chapters.title: Ray Confronts Denny
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Ray, knowing Denny knows, gives a speech about protecting the town, the team, Denny's scholarship chances. 'Some truths cost more than they're worth.' Denny wavers. Beat: inheritance of silence.

chapters.title: The Leak Backfires
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Someone leaks that 'The Locker' is a student; the board threatens expulsion and lawsuits against whoever it is. Oscar's mother finds the Maple Street key in his jacket. Beat: the walls closing.

chapters.title: Mother
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. His mother reveals she suspected Grandma Fairweather kept secrets—Grandma was the school secretary who made copies before she was fired in 1994. Oscar learns he inherited this fight. Beat: lineage of courage.

chapters.title: Coach Brandt's Version
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. The aging coach, dying of cancer, tells Oscar privately that he protected boys the only way he knew, and that Mateo's death broke something in him too. Not absolution—complication. Beat: the villain given a face.

chapters.title: Expulsion Hearing Notice
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The board suspends Oscar pending a hearing, citing 'unauthorized access to school property.' Denny is asked to testify about the annex break-in. Beat: loyalty put on the stand.

chapters.title: What Denny Says
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. At the hearing, Denny lies to protect Oscar—his first lie to an institution instead of a friend—and hates how easy it is. Ray sees straight through him. Beat: corruption touching the innocent.

chapters.title: The Town Divides
chapters.summary: Multi-POV mosaic: diner patrons, players, parents. Half the town wants the truth; half wants the football season left alone. Rosa Delgado organizes alumni. Beat: a community choosing sides.

chapters.title: The Fire
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The Maple Street house burns in the night—arson, unstated but obvious. The physical evidence survives because Oscar had digitized everything, but the loss lands like a threat delivered. Beat: fear made physical.

chapters.title: Anonymous No More
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The regional reporter, closing in, gives Oscar twenty-four hours before publishing the blogger's identity. Oscar decides to get ahead of it. Beat: the pivot from hiding to standing.

chapters.title: Signed
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar posts his name, face, and full account—including being the only out kid in Halloway—in one unflinching essay. The town wakes to it. Beat: terror transfigured into release.

chapters.title: Fallout
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. Classmates react—some embrace Oscar, some spit slurs, Ms. Okafor publicly defends him at cost to herself. Denny doesn't call. Beat: the true price of visibility.

chapters.title: State Investigators
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. With Oscar named, the state attorney general opens an inquiry; Priya's archived photos become evidence. Ray hires a lawyer. Beat: machinery finally turning toward justice.

chapters.title: Denny's Choice
chapters.summary: Denny's POV. Ray asks Denny to sign a statement discrediting Oscar. Denny looks at his father—the man who taught him to throw a spiral—and refuses, then walks out. Beat: breaking the inheritance.

chapters.title: The Gymnasium
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At a packed emergency forum, Oscar speaks—not about documents, but about every kid who learned to disappear in this building. Silence, then Rosa stands, then others. Beat: climax of voice.

chapters.title: Ray Resigns
chapters.summary: Ray's POV. Facing indictment, Ray resigns at a kitchen table, asking Denny if he's proud. Denny says, 'I'm sad. It's not the same thing.' Beat: power's unglamorous end.

chapters.title: Mateo's Name
chapters.summary: Oscar and Rosa's POV. The board votes to place Mateo Delgado's name on a memorial wall and void the old settlements' gag clauses. It's not enough. It's something. Beat: partial, honest repair.

chapters.title: The Hearing Reversed
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar's suspension is overturned; Ms. Okafor hands back his college essay with one note: 'Now it's true.' Oscar rewrites it in his own name. Beat: the frame closes on the opening question.

chapters.title: Graduation Practice
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Caps thrown in a hot gym, Denny beside him again—wordless, then not. Coach Brandt attends from a wheelchair and nods once at Oscar. Beat: reconciliation without erasure.

chapters.title: The Last Post
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar writes the blog's final entry: not an exposé but a letter to the next kid in a town of nine hundred who thinks invisibility is safety. Beat: passing the torch.

chapters.title: Maple Street, Spring
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The burned lot is cleared; Oscar plants something in the soil where the locker stood. Leaving for college in the fall, he no longer counts days—he lives them. Beat: quiet triumph.

chapters.title: What Truth You Carry
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, final chapter. On move-in day, Oscar reads his published essay aloud to his roommate—a stranger who simply says 'cool' and means it. Somewhere, another kid opens a locked door. Beat: belonging, finally unearned by suffering, freely found.
